# Open rows {#open-rows}

## Row variables

Open rows support row extension, decomposition, reusable type positions, and row-conditional
implementations. [A generic parameter that stands for a record is declared `record R`](#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-1).

> **Gap** GAP-TYPES-008

A `record`-kinded generic parameter used as `..R` abstracts over "the rest of a row" rather than a
concrete shape. The binder is `record R`; every use of its *row* is written `..R`,
distinguishing it from the record type `R` itself in every position a row can appear —
a record type's tail (`.{ .x: f64, ..R }`), a struct's own residual projection
(`Handle.{ ..R }`), and a generic argument (`Session<..R>`):

```metel
fun get_x<record R>(p: .{ .x: f64, ..R }) -> f64 { p.x }
```

<details>
<summary>Formal rules</summary>

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-1}

A generic parameter that stands for a record is declared `record R`; the *row* of such a
parameter is written `..R` (or anonymous `..`) — in a record type's tail, a struct's own
residual-projection tail, or generic-argument position. A bare identifier in any of these
type positions is the record type `R` itself, never its row; `R` and `..R` are therefore never
ambiguous with each other. The `row` kind and keyword do not exist. `..R` on a parameter
that is not `record`-kinded is a type error.

An open record type may occur in a reusable type position, including a function or
instance-method parameter, a return type, a local annotation, or a nominal field.
Its row tail is substituted and checked wherever the enclosing type is instantiated.

For a branded `record` type `R`, `.{ ..R }` is the anonymous record with the same
fields; `R` itself retains its brand. Converting an owned branded record to its
anonymous row consumes the branded value and transfers its fields. This conversion
is rejected if the branded type implements `Drop`, because it would bypass its
destructor. A borrowed open-row view does not consume or alter the borrowed value;
its brand remains available through the original value.

A struct's residual-projection tail (`Handle.{ .fd, ..R }`, `Handle.{ ..R }`) is narrower: it is
accepted only as the type of a function parameter, and anywhere else (a return type, an
annotation, a field, under `&`) it is a parse error naming that restriction. A row argument
to a nominal type (`Session<..R>`), an open record, or a closed projection (`Handle.{ .fd }`)
covers the same ground in those positions. A projection that names no fields
(`Handle.{ ..R }`) takes a whole struct, like `.{ ..R }`, and so does one that names fields
(`Handle.{ .fd, ..R }`); see [legality-3](#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-3).

A row argument is a row variable (`..R`), an anonymous `..`, or a **literal row**: an open or
closed record type written after `..`. `Req<..{ host: String, ..R }>` is `Req` at the row `R`
extended with `host`; `Req<..{ host: String }>` is `Req` at exactly that one field, and
`Req<..{}>` at the empty row. A literal row is the same type the checker infers for a record
literal with a spread, so a written return type and an inferred one agree. The labels it
adds must be provably absent from the tail, exactly as for a spread (`R: !{ host }`), and it is
accepted only where the generic parameter is declared `record`. An anonymous tail inside a literal
follows the positions in [legality-5](#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-5).

```metel
record Req<record R> { data: .{ ..R } }

fun empty() -> Req<..{}> { Req { data = .{} } }

fun add_host<record R: !{ .host }>(r: Req<..R>, h: String) -> Req<..{ .host: String, ..R }> {
    Req { data = .{ .host = h, ..r.data } }
}

extend<record R: .{ .host: String, .. }> Req<..R> {
    fun build(self) -> String { "GET " + self.data.host }
}

fun main() {
    assert(add_host(empty(), "a.com").build() == "GET a.com");
}
```

## Extension and removal

**Extension needs no operator** — the new label goes directly in the row literal:

```metel
RequestBuilder<.{ ..R, .auth: String }>
```

**Removal from an abstract row uses a rest pattern.** A `where` equation names both halves
and states how they compose, which simultaneously subsumes a row bound (`R = { token, ..Rest }`
already implies `R: { token, .. }`) and names the remainder:

```metel
extend<record R, record Rest> Session<..R>
where R = .{ .token: Token, ..Rest }
{
    fun authenticate(self) -> Session<..Rest> { ... }
}
```

The equation constrains the *type*. In a generic body, `{ token, ..rest }` consumes a record
and binds its unnamed fields as an owned anonymous record. A row spread (`.{ ..rest, .auth = a }`)
places an owned record's fields into a new record. The details and current implementation
limit are specified below.

Reading a field the equation promises is:

```metel
fun split<record R, record Rest>(p: .{ .token: i64, ..R }) -> i64
where R = .{ .extra: i64, ..Rest }
{
    p.token + p.extra
}

fun main() {
    assert(split(.{ .token = 1, .extra = 2, .other = 3 }) == 3);
}
```

For a rest pattern, the checker removes the explicitly named labels from the strongest
decomposition entailed by the scrutinee's type and declared row facts. Other known fields
and the open tail remain. Thus, if `S = .{ .token: Token, .extra: i64, ..Rest }`, then
`{ token, ..rest }` gives `rest: .{ .extra: i64, ..Rest }`.

[A presence-only bound such as
`R: { token, .. }` proves that `token` exists but does not determine the remainder type](../../expressions/patterns/struct-and-record-patterns.md#spec.expressions.record-rest-patterns.legality-1);
the pattern is rejected with a distinct “remainder type cannot be determined” diagnostic.

If all fields are removed from a closed row, the remainder has empty anonymous-record type
`.{}`, which is `()` ([the empty tuple](../tuples.md#spec.types.tuples.legality-2)). Bare `..` in a pattern remains discard-only and does not produce a value.

A record literal accepts at most one spread, including for concrete rows. A written label is an
addition when proven absent from the spread row, a replacement when proven present, and rejected when neither is proven. Initializers evaluate from
left to right, while field order/layout is determined by the resulting row/type, not initializer
order.

<details>
<summary>Formal rules</summary>

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-2}

A row literal's trailing `..R` (or anonymous `..`) extends that row with whatever
fields `R` carries. A `where R = .{ .label: Type, ..Rest }` equation decomposes a row
variable `R` into one named field and a remainder `Rest`, and simultaneously bounds `R`
to carry at least that field (equivalent to `R: .{ .label: Type, .. }`).

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-4}

A record literal contains at most one spread. Each explicitly initialized label is judged against the spread row: it is an addition when entailed
absent, a replacement when entailed present with type `T` (the replacement must have type `T`, and the result row is the spread row), and is rejected
when neither is entailed, which an abstract row requires a fact for. An absent-label fact is a closed row without the label, a decomposition whose
remainder excludes it, a label-only negative bound (`R: !{ .token }`) or a negative entry `!.token`; a present-label fact is a concrete row, a
decomposition, or a positive entry `.x` or `.x: T`. A typed negative bound such as `R: !{ .token: String }` is not an absent-label fact: it only rules
out that type. Spreading an owned record moves its fields into the result except the replaced ones, whose old values are dropped, and consumes the
source; when the record is not known `Discard`, every replaced field must be `Discard`. Spreading through a reference copies the fields only when every field that is
not replaced is provably `Copy`; otherwise it is rejected with `T0033`. Initializers evaluate left-to-right, while the resulting record layout is
determined by its row/type.

## Rows as nominal arguments

A row may also be the argument of a nominal type's own row parameter, written
`..R` in the argument list. A bound on that row (`where R = .{ .auth: String, .. }`) is
checked at each use:

```metel
record Builder<record R> { name: String, data: .{ ..R } }

fun auth_of<record R>(b: Builder<..R>) -> String where R = .{ .auth: String, .. } {
    b.data.auth
}

fun main() {
    let b := Builder { name = "req", data = .{ .auth = "tok", .retries = 3 } };
    assert(auth_of(b) == "tok");
}
```

[An argument whose row lacks a required label is rejected with `T0012`](row-bounds.md#spec.types.generics.row-bounds.legality-10):

<!-- doc-example: expect-fail reason="the argument's row has no `auth` field -- T0012 is the point" -->
```metel
record Builder<record R> { name: String, data: .{ ..R } }

fun auth_of<record R>(b: Builder<..R>) -> String where R = .{ .auth: String, .. } {
    b.data.auth
}

fun main() {
    let bare := Builder { name = "bare", data = .{ .retries = 1 } };
    let _ := auth_of(bare);
}
```

A tail-only parameter `.{ ..R }` transfers the entire owned row, and a parameter that names
fields (`.{ .f: T, ..R }`) takes the whole record too, so the two spellings accept the same
programs and an owned remainder may hold non-`Copy` fields.

## Width subtyping

**Width subtyping.** [A record with extra fields may be passed to a parameter that names
only some of them (`.{ .x: f64, ..R }`); the extras bind to `R`](#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-3). By value the parameter takes
the **whole** record: the callee owns the extra fields and may move, return or drop them, so
they need not be `Copy`:

```metel
fun get_x<record R>(p: .{ .x: i64, ..R }) -> i64 { p.x }

fun main() {
    let wide := .{ .x = 1, .name = "ada".to_string() };
    assert(get_x(wide) == 1);
}
```

Taking the record by reference does not move it, so the caller keeps every field:

```metel
fun get_x<record R>(p: &.{ .x: i64, ..R }) -> i64 { p.x }

fun main() {
    let wide := .{ .x = 1, .name = "ada" };
    assert(get_x(&wide) == 1);
    assert(wide.name == "ada");
}
```

Inside a generic body the extras are abstract, and the body owns them too, so it can pass
the parameter on by value with no bound. `where ..R: Copy` is only needed to *use* the row
more than once:

```metel
fun consume<record R>(p: .{ .x: i64, ..R }) -> i64 { p.x }

fun outer<record R>(s: .{ .x: i64, ..R }) -> i64 {
    consume(s) + 1
}

fun main() {
    assert(outer(.{ .x = 1, .k = "kept".to_string(), .flag = true }) == 2);
}
```

<details>
<summary>Formal rules</summary>

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-3}

A by-value parameter whose type has an open row tail (`.{ .x: Type, ..R }`, or
`Handle.{ .fd, ..R }`) takes its argument **whole**. The call needs only that the argument has
the named fields at the declared types; the fields the parameter does not name are the
callee's to move, return or drop, so they need not be `Copy`, and a generic body that
forwards such a parameter to another by-value open-row function needs no `where ..R: Copy`.
A parameter taken through a reference (`&{ .x: Type, ..R }`, `&var`) never moves the value
and forgets nothing.

A nominal argument whose type has a `Drop` impl is the one exception: dropping it inside the
callee needs drop dispatch against a narrowed residual, which is not
implemented, so passing it to an open-row parameter is rejected with `T0036`. A plain record
that only *contains* a `Drop` value is unaffected.

## Anonymous tails

An open record with an anonymous tail (`.{ .x: T, .. }`) is not accepted everywhere; see
[legality-5](#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-5). Three limits are recorded as gaps.

> **Gap** GAP-TYPES-010

[A function cannot return an open record while hiding its extra fields: an anonymous tail in a
return type is `T0032`](#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-5). Omit the return type, write the record in full, or name a row that comes
from an argument.

> **Gap** GAP-TYPES-011

A written function type cannot say it accepts any record with at least some fields. A named row
(`|.{ .x: T, ..R }| -> U`) works for callbacks over records of one shape.

> **Gap** GAP-TYPES-012

A record or struct field cannot have an open-record type with an anonymous tail; give the record
a row parameter instead.

<details>
<summary>Formal rules</summary>

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.generics.open-rows.legality-5}

An open record type whose tail is **anonymous**, `.{ .x: T, .. }` or `.{ .. }`, denotes a record
with at least the named fields and a remainder that is a **fresh row at each occurrence**. It
is accepted:

- as the type of a function or method parameter;
- as the annotation of a `let` or `var` binding;
- as the annotation of a closure parameter; and
- as the right-hand side of a type alias, where each use of the alias is its own fresh row.

In a `let` or `var` annotation the fresh row is solved by the initializer, so the binding has
the initializer's type and every one of its fields stays readable; the annotation names the
fields that must be present and does not narrow the value. The field types written in the
annotation apply to the initializer, so `.{ .x: u8, .. }` makes `x` a `u8`. A closure whose parameter carries
such an annotation is polymorphic in that row: each call instantiates it afresh, so one closure
accepts records of different shapes.

```metel
fun main() {
    let a: .{ .x: i64, .. } := .{ .x = 1, .y = "s".to_string() };
    assert(a.y == "s");

    let get := |p: .{ .x: i64, .. }| { p.x };
    assert(get(.{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }) == 1);
    assert(get(.{ .x = 5 }) == 5);
    assert(get(.{ .x = 7, .flag = true }) == 7);
}
```

An open record with an anonymous tail is rejected with `T0032` as a **return type**, inside a
**written function type**, and as a **record or struct field**. In a return type or function type
the tail has no construct that solves it, and a field's type would differ between values of one
nominal type. A named tail (`.{ .x: T, ..R }`, `R` declared `record`) is not affected by this rule
and is accepted wherever `R` is in scope.

<!-- doc-example: expect-fail reason="an anonymous open record has no solver in a return type -- T0032 is the point" -->
```metel
fun make() -> .{ .x: i64, .. } {
    .{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }
}

fun main() {
    let _ := make();
}
```
